title: What Klopp's Liverpool Era Meant for English Football — and What Comes Next
summary: Jurgen Klopp's nine years at Liverpool redefined what English football could be: intense, emotional, and built on a system that turned good players into great ones. We look at the legacy of one of the game's most transformative managers.
content:
When Jurgen Klopp arrived at Liverpool in October 2015, the club was drifting. Brendan Rodgers' promising project had collapsed. The owners were patient but concerned. And Liverpool, one of English football's great institutions, was watching their rivals pull away while they stood still.

What followed over the next nine years was one of the most remarkable managerial tenures in the history of the game. Klopp did not simply win trophies — though he won plenty. He changed the DNA of a football club, rebuilt a fanbase's belief, and in doing so, changed how English football thought about what a team could be.

The System

Klopp's Liverpool was built on gegenpressing — the immediate, intense counter-press the moment possession was lost. The idea, developed in his years at Borussia Dortmund, was deceptively simple: win the ball back immediately after losing it, before the opponent can reorganise. Done well, it creates chaos for the opposition and momentum for your team. Done poorly, it leaves enormous spaces to exploit.

What Liverpool did under Klopp was execute this system at a level of intensity and coordination that had rarely been seen in English football. Players pressed in coordinated units, cutting off passing lanes, anticipating where the ball would go. The front three — in their peak years, Salah, Firmino, and Mane — were among the best pressing forwards the game has ever seen.

The Signings That Made It Work

Klopp's Liverpool was also defined by extraordinary recruitment. Mohamed Salah arrived from Roma for £36.9 million — a figure that looked expensive at the time and laughable within twelve months. Virgil van Dijk transformed the defence, turning a liability into the foundation of one of the best backlines in Europe. Alisson Becker made the goalkeeper position a strength rather than a weakness.

These were not random signings. Each player was identified because they fitted the system perfectly — technically capable, physically extraordinary, and mentally equipped for the demands Klopp placed on his squad.

Football is about emotion. If you don't feel anything when you're winning and losing, you can't be in this job. And if the players can feel what the fans feel, and the fans can feel what the players feel, then you have something special. That's what I tried to build at Liverpool.

The Trophies

The haul was extraordinary: the Premier League title that ended a 30-year wait; the Champions League won in Madrid; the FA Cup, the League Cup, the UEFA Super Cup, the Club World Cup. Liverpool under Klopp became the first club in history to win all six major trophies available to an English side.

But the trophies do not capture everything. The 97-point Premier League season that still wasn't enough to beat Manchester City. The 2018-19 Champions League run. The comeback against Barcelona at Anfield. These were moments that transcended sport — that created memories for millions of people that have nothing to do with the actual silverware.

What Comes Next

Klopp's departure in 2024, announced with characteristic honesty as a decision made because he had given everything he had, left a gap that his successor Arne Slot has had to fill. Slot's Liverpool have shown continuity of method — the pressing game remains, the squad is largely unchanged — but also the first signs of his own tactical identity asserting itself.

The Klopp era's legacy is not simply what it won. It is what it proved: that a team built on a clear idea, executed with intensity and conviction, can compete with the richest clubs in the world and beat them. That is a lesson English football will not forget.
